script.opening: (Anxious, lowering her voice, glancing away from the screen.) "I need to tell someone, and I don't know if I'm doing the right thing … My brother's daughter — my niece, she's 7 — they're taking her 'back home' for the summer. In our family, that's when girls are … cut. I went through it myself. I can't let it happen to her, but I don't want to destroy my family. What do I do?"

facts.text: If asked, will give details: "Yes, I can give you all that." Niece Amina Yusuf, 7, lives with her parents (Halima's brother and his wife) in the same town; goes to the local primary school; Halima knows the address and the school.

"They said the summer holidays. I don't know the exact date or if they've booked yet." School breaks up in 4 weeks. Her mother (Amina's grandmother) has been saying it is "time" and a big family celebration is planned.
"It's what happens in our family at that age. It's what happened to me when I was taken back." Heard the grandmother talking about a "woman who does it".
"I don't know about everyone. I'd have to think." Amina has a 4-year-old sister. Her own daughter is 10 — Halima will never let her go.
"I don't think they'd hurt me. But they'd never speak to me again." Lives with her husband (supportive) and daughter.
Cut at age 8. If asked: painful periods and sex, has never told a doctor. "Maybe later. I've never talked about it."
"That my brother goes to prison and the family blames me. And that nobody believes me and she gets cut anyway." "Will they tell my brother it was me?"

Frightened, ashamed, determined. Expected the doctor might act: "Yes. I knew you might have to do something." If the doctor only advises her to talk to her brother, look lost (the trap). Relieved when the doctor says professionals will take it from here. Contact: "Yes, this mobile is fine."

ice.ideas: "They will cut her on the trip home this summer."
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — terror for Amina; fear of being blamed and losing her family; her own unspoken trauma from being cut.
ice.expectations: "Stop it happening. Without it all being my fault."

cues: "I went through it myself." — her own FGM; return to it with care.
"I don't want to destroy my family." — divided loyalty.
"Will they tell my brother it was me?" — needs honest information.

checkpoints.text: Recognises a girl at risk of FGM as a CHILD-PROTECTION emergency — serious harm/child abuse that overrides confidentiality and family-loyalty considerations — and treats planned summer travel "home" as high-risk

Acts on the mandatory SAFEGUARDING duty: makes a prompt referral to CHILDREN’S SOCIAL CARE (police via 999 if travel is imminent), gathering proportionate information but NOT managing it alone or delaying to investigate, and involves the safeguarding lead

Knows the LAW: FGM (and taking/arranging to take a UK girl abroad for it) is illegal; FGM PROTECTION ORDERS can prevent travel (applied for by the girl or the local authority, or by others with the court’s leave); the statutory mandatory-reporting duty applies to KNOWN FGM in under-18s (police), at-risk cases via safeguarding referral
Is culturally sensitive and compassionate WITHOUT colluding — clear that FGM is child abuse regardless of cultural framing and that culture is no justification
Considers the WIDER FAMILY (other girls at risk) and ensures the referral captures this, while handling the aunt’s information appropriately

Holds the AUNT with compassion — acknowledges her courage, distress, divided loyalty and her own trauma as a survivor — and reassures her that protecting the child is right, recording her own FGM (Enhanced Dataset, explained to her; not a police report, as she is an adult)
Explains what will happen and that professionals will handle it, so she is not left carrying the burden, and signposts support for her

Safety-nets and acts: prompt safeguarding referral with documentation, support/signposting for the aunt (FGM services, survivor support), consideration of FGMPO/urgency (999 if travel is imminent), the aunt’s own FGM recorded in her notes and the Enhanced Dataset, and follow-up — decisive child protection with compassion

worked.txt: "Thank you for telling me — that took real courage, and you are absolutely doing the right thing by your niece. Let me help you carry this; you won’t be dealing with it alone."
"What you’re describing — a girl at risk of being cut — is something we take extremely seriously. FGM is illegal here, it’s a form of harm to a child, and I have a duty to act to protect her."

"I can’t keep this just between us, and I shouldn’t try to handle it alone — I need to involve the people whose job is to protect children, today. There are also legal orders — usually applied for by the council — that can stop her being taken abroad, even surrendering passports, to keep her safe."

"Can you tell me her name and age, her parents, and when and where they’re planning to travel? … And are there other girls in the family who might also be at risk? That helps the team protect them all."

"I understand this is your family and your own painful history — I’m not judging anyone. But protecting this little girl comes first, and tradition can never justify harming a child. You’re doing right by her."

"I’ll make the referral now and keep you informed. There’s also support for you — as someone who went through this yourself. If you hear the travel is sooner than thought, tell me immediately, because we may need to act fast — and if they are about to leave, call 999. I’ll also note what you’ve told me about yourself in your own record; GP practices have to add that to a national NHS FGM dataset, which doesn’t involve the police, and I can refer you to a specialist FGM clinic."

f.learning: A disclosure that a girl is at risk of female genital mutilation — here a 7-year-old to be taken abroad in the summer when cutting traditionally occurs — is a child-protection emergency: a girl at risk of FGM is a child at risk of serious harm, FGM is a form of child abuse and illegal in the UK, and this overrides the usual confidentiality and family-loyalty considerations, with time critical if travel is imminent. The mandatory duty is to act, not deliberate: take the disclosure with the utmost seriousness, gather proportionate information (the child’s name and age, parents, when and where they are travelling, the specific risk, and whether other girls in the family are at risk), and make a prompt safeguarding referral to children’s social care (and the police via 999 if travel is imminent or there is immediate danger) — you do not manage this alone, merely advise the relative, or delay to investigate yourself — involving the practice safeguarding lead. Know the legal framework (FGM Act 2003, as amended): FGM and taking or arranging to take a UK girl abroad for it are illegal; FGM Protection Orders can be obtained to prevent travel (including surrendering passports) and protect a specific child — by the girl or the local authority without the court’s leave, or by anyone else (including the police or a relative) with it; and the statutory mandatory-reporting duty for regulated professionals applies specifically to KNOWN/identified FGM in a girl under 18 (report to police), while a child merely at risk goes through the safeguarding-referral route. Be culturally sensitive and compassionate — especially as the aunt is herself a survivor acting protectively against her own family — but never collude, holding absolute clarity that FGM is child abuse regardless of cultural framing and that tradition is no justification. Support the aunt (acknowledge her courage and divided loyalty, reassure her she is doing right, signpost FGM specialist and survivor support, and record her own disclosed FGM in her notes and the mandatory FGM Enhanced Dataset — explained to her, no consent needed, and not a police report for an adult), consider the wider family, and document carefully. The hidden agenda is her torment between protecting the child and loyalty to/fear of family, plus her own trauma; respond decisively to the child-protection duty while holding her with compassion and not leaving the burden on her.

knowledge.guideline: FGM Act 2003 (as amended by the Serious Crime Act 2015) · Multi-agency statutory guidance on FGM (Home Office, updated July 2020) · Mandatory reporting of FGM: procedural information (Home Office/DH) · FGM risk and safeguarding guidance for professionals (DH) · Working Together to Safeguard Children (HM Government, 2026)
knowledge.summary: A girl at risk of FGM is a child at risk of significant harm. The GP acts on it the same day through a safeguarding referral; the mandatory police-reporting duty is for known FGM in under-18s, not risk.

points.t: FGM Act 2003: performing FGM, or aiding or procuring it, is an offence with a maximum of 14 years’ imprisonment. Since the 2015 amendments the law covers acts done abroad by or to UK nationals or people habitually resident in the UK, so taking a girl abroad for FGM is an offence.

Section 3A (added 2015): a person responsible for a girl under 16 when FGM is committed against her can be guilty of failing to protect her (maximum 7 years). Responsibility can include relatives looking after her over a holiday.

A civil court order to protect a girl at risk. It can require surrender of passports and ban travel. The girl, a local authority (without the court’s leave) or any other person with the court’s leave can apply. Breach is a criminal offence (maximum 5 years).

Regulated health and social care professionals and teachers in England and Wales must report to the police (usually 101) when a girl under 18 discloses FGM or they see physical signs of it. Report within one month, and best practice is by the end of the next working day. The duty does not cover girls at risk or suspected cases: those go through local safeguarding procedures.

Multi-agency statutory guidance: refer to children’s social care (and police if there is immediate danger, via 999) following local safeguarding procedures; involve the practice safeguarding lead; do not approach the family yourself. Imminent travel makes it urgent.

points.h: The adult who discloses her own FGM
points.t: An adult woman with FGM is not reported to the police. Record it in her notes and submit to the FGM Enhanced Dataset, which is mandatory for GP practices; consent is not needed, but explain it to her. Offer referral to specialist FGM services.

dg.d: Checked privacy on video; open question; let her disclose at her own pace.
Family context, her fear of blame and breakdown, her own history and her safety.
Gathered name, parents, address, travel dates and destination, and other girls at risk; did not investigate further.
Risk indicators: family tradition, age, planned trip to a practising community in the summer, and an affected close relative.
Recognised significant harm to a child; considered imminent travel (999) and the aunt’s own safety.
Stated clearly: a child at risk of FGM, a safeguarding concern requiring referral, not mandatory reporting.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.
Used information already available in the notes/referral; did not re-ask what was already documented or said.

dg.t: Finishes data gathering in good time
dg.d: History, ICE, psychosocial context and red-flag screen completed by ~6–7 minutes, leaving time for explanation and a shared plan.

cm.d: Same-day referral to children’s social care with the safeguarding lead; FGM Protection Order explained; no approach to the family.
Recorded the aunt’s own FGM and the Enhanced Dataset; offered FGM clinic and psychological support.
Safe contact number; call 999 if travel imminent; documented; follow-up call arranged.

cm.t: Uses psychosocial information in the plan
cm.d: Tailored the plan to the patient’s circumstances, beliefs and practical barriers rather than giving a generic plan.

cm.t: Shares risks and safety of options
cm.d: Explained the benefits and risks of the options clearly, as concrete terms or numbers where possible.
Acknowledged autonomy, capacity, confidentiality, safeguarding and any fitness-to-drive/work or duty-of-care implications relevant to this case.
Moved efficiently through the consultation so all key areas were covered within the time without getting stuck.

ro.d: Picked up “I went through it myself” and “I don’t want to destroy my family” and responded to both.
Idea (the trip is for cutting), concern (family blame, not being believed), expectation (stop it without it being her fault).
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.
Told the patient why a question, examination or test was being done — transparent reasoning throughout.
Explained the working diagnosis or analysis in plain language the patient could understand.

ro.t: Shares and uses ICE in the plan
ro.d: Addressed the patient’s specific concern — terror for Amina; fear of being blamed and losing her family; her own unspoken trauma from being cut — directly within the plan, rather than noting it and moving on.
Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.

model.text: Hello, Ms Yusuf, I’m Dr Patel. Are you somewhere you can talk privately? Take your time and tell me what’s on your mind.
model.why: Checks privacy on video and opens gently

model.text: I need to tell someone, and I don’t know if I’m doing the right thing. My brother’s daughter, my niece, she’s 7. They’re taking her ‘back home’ for the summer. In our family, that’s when girls are… cut. I went through it myself. I can’t let it happen to her, but I don’t want to destroy my family. What do I do?
Thank you for telling me. That took real courage, and you are doing the right thing by her. I’m going to help you with this, and you won’t be carrying it on your own.
model.why: Acknowledges courage and relieves her of the burden

model.text: I’ve been sick with worry about it.

I can hear that. I want to be honest with you from the start: what you’ve described is a child at risk of serious harm, and I have a duty to act to protect her. I’ll explain everything as we go. First I need to understand the details. Is that okay?
model.why: Honest about the duty early, and sets the agenda

model.text: Yes. I knew you might have to do something.
Can you tell me her name, her parents’ names and where they live?
model.why: Gathers the identifying details the referral needs

model.text: Yes, I can give you all that.
When are they planning to travel, and where to? Do you know if tickets are booked?
model.why: Establishes timing, as imminent travel changes the urgency

model.text: They said the summer holidays. I don’t know the exact date or if they’ve booked yet.
What makes you think she will be cut on this trip? Has anyone said so?
model.why: Clarifies the specific risk indicators without investigating

model.text: It’s what happens in our family at that age. It’s what happened to me when I was taken back.
Are there other girls in the family, here or anywhere else, who might also be at risk?
I don’t know about everyone. I’d have to think.
That’s fine; social care will ask about that too. And are you safe yourself? Could telling me put you at risk from anyone in the family?
I don’t think they’d hurt me. But they’d never speak to me again.
That’s a painful thing to face. What’s your biggest worry about what happens next?
model.why: Explores her fear of family breakdown

model.text: That my brother goes to prison and the family blames me. And that nobody believes me and she gets cut anyway.
Both of those make sense. What were you hoping I could do?
I don’t know. Stop it happening. Without it all being my fault.

I understand this is your family, and I’m not judging you or your community. But cutting a girl is illegal in this country and is harm to a child, whatever the tradition. It is also illegal to take a girl abroad to have it done. Protecting her has to come first.
model.why: Culturally sensitive, clear on the law, no collusion

model.text: I know. That’s why I came.

So I’ll make a referral to children’s social care today, and I’ll involve our practice safeguarding lead. Their job is to protect her. They can work with the police, and if needed they can apply to a court for a protection order, which can stop her being taken abroad, including handing in passports.
model.why: Same-day safeguarding referral and explains FGM Protection Orders

model.text: Will they tell my brother it was me?

I can’t promise nobody will work it out, but I will tell them you’re worried about your safety and your family, and they will think about how they approach this. I won’t go to your brother myself. You haven’t done anything wrong: you’re protecting her.
model.why: Honest about confidentiality limits and supports her

model.text: You also said you went through this yourself. I’d like to record that in your notes, which we do for every woman who has had FGM, and it is sent to a national NHS dataset that is only published as anonymous figures. That is not a police report — you’re not in any trouble. Would you like me to refer you to a specialist FGM clinic, or to someone to talk to?
model.why: Records her own FGM, explains recording is not reporting, and offers survivor support

model.text: Maybe later. I’ve never talked about it.

The offer stays open. If you learn the travel date, or that it has been brought forward, tell me or the police straight away — if she is about to be taken, call 999. Can I have a number that’s safe to call you on?
model.why: Specific urgent safety-net and safe contact

model.text: Yes, this mobile is fine.
Let me check we’re clear. What will happen after this call?
You’re telling social care today, they may involve the police and a court order, and I call 999 if she’s about to go.
That’s right. I’ll document everything carefully and call you in the next few days to see how you are. You did the right thing today.
model.why: Documentation and planned follow-up for the discloser

social.t: FGM is often upheld by family pressure and a belief that it protects the girl. The discloser may lose family relationships; offer ongoing support.
Disclosure may bring up her own trauma. Offer referral to specialist FGM services and psychological support at her pace.

legal.t: Offences apply abroad for UK nationals and residents; failing to protect a girl under 16 is an offence; victims have lifelong anonymity; FGM Protection Orders can prevent travel.

Known FGM in a girl under 18 (disclosed or seen) must be reported to the police by the regulated professional personally, within one month and ideally by the end of the next working day. It does not apply to girls at risk.
Working Together to Safeguard Children (2026) and the multi-agency statutory guidance on FGM (2020): refer at-risk girls to children’s social care; call 999 if the danger is immediate.

professional.t: GMC Confidentiality (2017): disclosure without consent is justified where it is necessary to protect a child from serious harm. Tell her what you will share and why.
GMC Protecting children and young people (2012): all doctors must act on concerns about a child, including children who are not their patients.
Record the disclosure, what you did and who you told. Record her own FGM and submit to the FGM Enhanced Dataset.

community.t: The Home Office “Statement opposing FGM” can be given to families to take abroad. The NSPCC FGM helpline and specialist FGM clinics support families and survivors.

redFlags: Travel booked or imminent — 999 and urgent social care referral
Other girls in the family at the same age or younger
Threats to the discloser or signs of honour-based abuse
Any sign the niece has already been cut — this becomes a mandatory police report
psychosocial: Her position in the family and fear of being blamed
Her own experience of FGM and its effects on her
ice: Idea: “The summer trip is when girls in our family are cut”
Concern: destroying the family, being blamed, not being believed
Expectation: to stop it happening without it being her fault

playbook.diagnosis: “What you’ve told me means your niece is at risk of serious harm. That is a safeguarding concern I must act on today.”
playbook.diagnosisLay: “You’ve raised the alarm. Now the people whose job it is to protect children take over, so the weight isn’t on your shoulders any more.”

management.reflectIce: “You’re afraid of losing your family and being blamed. Protecting her is not betraying them. You are doing what the law and she both need.”
management.psychosocial: Plan safe contact, don’t let her confront the family, and offer her own FGM support when she is ready.
sharedPlan: Referral to children’s social care today; involve the practice safeguarding lead
Social care and police can seek an FGM Protection Order to stop travel
Record her own FGM in her notes and the Enhanced Dataset; offer FGM clinic referral
safetyNet: Travel imminent or brought forward — call 999
Follow-up call in a few days; document everything

pitfalls.intro: This station is failed on law and on action. Candidates mix up mandatory reporting with safeguarding referral, delay, or ask the aunt to handle it herself.

items.fail: Saying the mandatory reporting duty applies and that you will “report it to the police” as the only action.
items.why: The duty covers known FGM in a girl under 18. For a girl at risk, the statutory guidance route is a safeguarding referral to children’s social care.
items.fix: “I’m referring her to children’s social care today; they work with the police and can apply for a protection order.”

items.fail: Agreeing to wait until she finds out more, or advising her to talk to her brother.
items.why: Delay and alerting the family can lead to the girl being taken abroad sooner.
items.fix: Act today, and ask her not to confront anyone.

items.fail: Not asking about other girls in the family or the travel date.
items.why: The referral needs these facts, and siblings may be at the same risk.
items.fix: Ask who, when, where, and whether any other girls could be affected.

items.fail: Talking about “your culture” in a way that sounds judgemental, or accepting it as a reason to hold back.
items.why: Both lose marks: judging alienates her, and collusion fails the child.
items.fix: “I’m not judging your family. But no tradition can make harming a child acceptable.”

items.fail: Promising complete confidentiality or that nobody will know it was her.
items.fix: Be honest about what you share and why, and tell social care about her safety concerns.

items.fail: Forgetting that she disclosed her own FGM.
items.why: She is a survivor with her own health needs, and recording is required.
items.fix: Record it, explain that recording is not reporting, and offer specialist support.

Name, parents, address, when and where, other girls, her own safety. Don’t interrogate.
Fear of blame and family breakdown, fear of not being believed.
Illegal including abroad; referral to children’s social care today; safeguarding lead; FGM Protection Order; limits of confidentiality.
Record her own FGM; offer support; 999 if travel imminent; safe number; teach-back.

wordPics.fail: Keeps it confidential or tells her to talk to her brother; says the GP must “report it to the police under mandatory reporting” for a girl not yet cut, or does nothing; no referral; judges the family or colludes with “it’s their culture”.
wordPics.pass: Recognises a child at risk; makes a prompt referral to children’s social care; explains that FGM is illegal including abroad; is kind to the aunt; gives some safety-net.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: gathers exactly what the referral needs; checks for other girls and for the aunt’s safety; explains FGM Protection Orders; correctly separates mandatory reporting (known FGM under 18) from at-risk referral; records the aunt’s own FGM and offers her support; is honest about confidentiality; gives a 999 plan for imminent travel.

avoid.dont: "Let’s keep this between us for now and see what happens."
avoid.instead: "I can’t keep this just between us, because a child could be seriously harmed. I’ll make a referral today and explain every step."
avoid.why: Delay can mean the child is taken abroad and cut.

avoid.dont: "I have to report this to the police under the mandatory reporting law."
avoid.instead: "I need to refer this to children’s social care today; they work with the police to protect her."
avoid.why: Mandatory reporting covers known FGM in a girl under 18. A child at risk goes through safeguarding referral.

avoid.dont: "Why don’t you talk to your brother and try to change his mind?"
avoid.instead: "Please don’t confront anyone. Leave that to the professionals, who can do it safely."
avoid.why: Alerting the family can bring travel forward and put the aunt at risk.

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: FGM Act 2003 (as amended by the Serious Crime Act 2015) · Multi-agency statutory guidance on FGM (Home Office, updated July 2020) · Mandatory reporting of FGM: procedural information (Home Office/DH) · FGM risk and safeguarding guidance for professionals (DH) · Working Together to Safeguard Children (HM Government, 2026)
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: A girl at risk of FGM is a child at risk of significant harm. The GP acts on it the same day through a safeguarding referral; the mandatory police-reporting duty is for known FGM in under-18s, not risk.

points.t: FGM Act 2003: performing FGM, or aiding or procuring it, is an offence with a maximum of 14 years’ imprisonment. Since the 2015 amendments the law covers acts done abroad by or to UK nationals or people habitually resident in the UK, so taking a girl abroad for FGM is an offence.

Section 3A (added 2015): a person responsible for a girl under 16 when FGM is committed against her can be guilty of failing to protect her (maximum 7 years). Responsibility can include relatives looking after her over a holiday.

A civil court order to protect a girl at risk. It can require surrender of passports and ban travel. The girl, a local authority (without the court’s leave) or any other person with the court’s leave can apply. Breach is a criminal offence (maximum 5 years).

Regulated health and social care professionals and teachers in England and Wales must report to the police (usually 101) when a girl under 18 discloses FGM or they see physical signs of it. Report within one month, and best practice is by the end of the next working day. The duty does not cover girls at risk or suspected cases: those go through local safeguarding procedures.

Multi-agency statutory guidance: refer to children’s social care (and police if there is immediate danger, via 999) following local safeguarding procedures; involve the practice safeguarding lead; do not approach the family yourself. Imminent travel makes it urgent.

points.h: The adult who discloses her own FGM
points.t: An adult woman with FGM is not reported to the police. Record it in her notes and submit to the FGM Enhanced Dataset, which is mandatory for GP practices; consent is not needed, but explain it to her. Offer referral to specialist FGM services.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Checked privacy on video; open question; let her disclose at her own pace.
Family context, her fear of blame and breakdown, her own history and her safety.
Picked up “I went through it myself” and “I don’t want to destroy my family” and responded to both.
Idea (the trip is for cutting), concern (family blame, not being believed), expectation (stop it without it being her fault).
Gathered name, parents, address, travel dates and destination, and other girls at risk; did not investigate further.
Risk indicators: family tradition, age, planned trip to a practising community in the summer, and an affected close relative.
Recognised significant harm to a child; considered imminent travel (999) and the aunt’s own safety.
Stated clearly: a child at risk of FGM, a safeguarding concern requiring referral, not mandatory reporting.
Same-day referral to children’s social care with the safeguarding lead; FGM Protection Order explained; no approach to the family.
Recorded the aunt’s own FGM and the Enhanced Dataset; offered FGM clinic and psychological support.
Safe contact number; call 999 if travel imminent; documented; follow-up call arranged.

social.t: FGM is often upheld by family pressure and a belief that it protects the girl. The discloser may lose family relationships; offer ongoing support.
Disclosure may bring up her own trauma. Offer referral to specialist FGM services and psychological support at her pace.

legal.t: Offences apply abroad for UK nationals and residents; failing to protect a girl under 16 is an offence; victims have lifelong anonymity; FGM Protection Orders can prevent travel.

Known FGM in a girl under 18 (disclosed or seen) must be reported to the police by the regulated professional personally, within one month and ideally by the end of the next working day. It does not apply to girls at risk.
Working Together to Safeguard Children (2026) and the multi-agency statutory guidance on FGM (2020): refer at-risk girls to children’s social care; call 999 if the danger is immediate.

professional.t: GMC Confidentiality (2017): disclosure without consent is justified where it is necessary to protect a child from serious harm. Tell her what you will share and why.
GMC Protecting children and young people (2012): all doctors must act on concerns about a child, including children who are not their patients.
Record the disclosure, what you did and who you told. Record her own FGM and submit to the FGM Enhanced Dataset.

community.t: The Home Office “Statement opposing FGM” can be given to families to take abroad. The NSPCC FGM helpline and specialist FGM clinics support families and survivors.

redFlags: Travel booked or imminent — 999 and urgent social care referral
Other girls in the family at the same age or younger
Threats to the discloser or signs of honour-based abuse
Any sign the niece has already been cut — this becomes a mandatory police report
psychosocial: Her position in the family and fear of being blamed
Her own experience of FGM and its effects on her
ice: Idea: “The summer trip is when girls in our family are cut”
Concern: destroying the family, being blamed, not being believed
Expectation: to stop it happening without it being her fault

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: “What you’ve told me means your niece is at risk of serious harm. That is a safeguarding concern I must act on today.”
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “You’ve raised the alarm. Now the people whose job it is to protect children take over, so the weight isn’t on your shoulders any more.”

management.reflectIce: “You’re afraid of losing your family and being blamed. Protecting her is not betraying them. You are doing what the law and she both need.”
management.psychosocial: Plan safe contact, don’t let her confront the family, and offer her own FGM support when she is ready.
sharedPlan: Referral to children’s social care today; involve the practice safeguarding lead
Social care and police can seek an FGM Protection Order to stop travel
Record her own FGM in her notes and the Enhanced Dataset; offer FGM clinic referral
safetyNet: Travel imminent or brought forward — call 999
Follow-up call in a few days; document everything

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station is failed on law and on action. Candidates mix up mandatory reporting with safeguarding referral, delay, or ask the aunt to handle it herself.

items.fail: Saying the mandatory reporting duty applies and that you will “report it to the police” as the only action.
items.why: The duty covers known FGM in a girl under 18. For a girl at risk, the statutory guidance route is a safeguarding referral to children’s social care.
items.fix: “I’m referring her to children’s social care today; they work with the police and can apply for a protection order.”

items.fail: Agreeing to wait until she finds out more, or advising her to talk to her brother.
items.why: Delay and alerting the family can lead to the girl being taken abroad sooner.
items.fix: Act today, and ask her not to confront anyone.

items.fail: Not asking about other girls in the family or the travel date.
items.why: The referral needs these facts, and siblings may be at the same risk.
items.fix: Ask who, when, where, and whether any other girls could be affected.

items.fail: Talking about “your culture” in a way that sounds judgemental, or accepting it as a reason to hold back.
items.why: Both lose marks: judging alienates her, and collusion fails the child.
items.fix: “I’m not judging your family. But no tradition can make harming a child acceptable.”

items.fail: Promising complete confidentiality or that nobody will know it was her.
items.fix: Be honest about what you share and why, and tell social care about her safety concerns.

items.fail: Forgetting that she disclosed her own FGM.
items.why: She is a survivor with her own health needs, and recording is required.
items.fix: Record it, explain that recording is not reporting, and offer specialist support.
